method: The Referrer-Policy header and the referrerpolicy attribute both name one of eight policies, and the specification's determine-request's-referrer algorithm maps a policy, the page URL and the target URL to either no header, the origin, or the full URL. The page first strips what a referrer never carries: the fragment, any username and password, and a port that is the default for the scheme (80 for http, 443 for https). It lowercases the host and keeps an IPv6 literal in brackets. The full form is scheme, host, port, path and query, with an empty path written as a slash; the origin form is scheme, host and port followed by a slash, as the specification requires so that the value is a valid URL. A request is same-origin when scheme, host and port all match. A downgrade is a page on https and a target on http only: an http page sending to an https target is an upgrade, not a downgrade, so no-referrer-when-downgrade keeps the full URL there. no-referrer sends nothing; no-referrer-when-downgrade sends the full URL except on a downgrade; same-origin sends the full URL only within the origin; origin always sends the origin; strict-origin sends the origin but not on a downgrade; origin-when-cross-origin sends the full URL within the origin and the origin otherwise, including downgrades; strict-origin-when-cross-origin sends the full URL within the origin, the origin across origins, and nothing on a downgrade; unsafe-url always sends the full URL. An empty policy falls back to no-referrer-when-downgrade, while browsers use strict-origin-when-cross-origin as their own default when a page sets nothing. Redirects are not chained here: the header always describes the document that started the request, so one page and one target are enough. Inputs accept http and https URLs in plain ASCII without spaces; everything else is refused rather than guessed. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.
